units.text: 01. A regularity is not yet a law

All the keys on my table are cold. If I declared this finding ‘the first law of living-room metals’, there would be an immediate argument against it: I can heat one of the keys. But the problem runs deeper. Even if nobody ever heated them, the sentence would remain an accidental description of a collection, not an explanation of how metals behave.

A law claims more than fidelity to an inventory. It concerns stable relationships and what would happen in situations different from actual ones: counterfactuals. This ‘if’ connects law to possibilities, not merely completed facts. The exact relationship between laws and counterfactuals remains disputed (Carroll, 2020) .

Take a spring. Within a certain deformation range, we can construct a model in which restoring force is proportional to extension. The model does not say that every elastic object behaves this way under all circumstances. Stretch the spring too far and the relationship ceases to be useful. We discover a domain limit, not nature’s decision to become unlawful.

This yields a practical question worth asking alongside every law taught in school: under what conditions can it be used? A formula without a domain resembles a medicine without indications and contraindications. It can be correct in form and misused in the world.

Four things must also be separated. An observation is a situated result: the instrument recorded a value. A regularity is a pattern among results. A law is a relationship to which we attribute a certain stability and generality. A theory is a structure of concepts, assumptions and relationships organizing explanations and predictions. A theory does not turn into a law after accumulating enough confirmations, like an employee being promoted. The two words serve different functions.

A model is a selective representation used for a problem. It may contain laws, approximations and conventions. A subway map is not false because it fails to preserve all distances; it is useful because it eliminates details unsuited to its purpose. A map for evacuating a building must preserve different relationships, however. Evaluating a model also means asking what information it must conserve.

Here the first ambiguity of realism appears. Are the letters in the formula real? They are signs produced by humans. Is the described relationship real? It may be: two teams can use different notation and build devices that work the same way. Is there, additionally, an entity called a ‘law’ compelling things to behave that way? This is a further metaphysical thesis. The formula’s success does not automatically decide it.

Confusing these levels produces two exaggerations. The first says: because equations are invented, the world they describe is invented. But a house’s address is also a convention, without making its walls conventional. The second says: because some equations work remarkably well, they are precisely the language in which the universe was written. This conclusion is not mandatory either. Multiple representations can capture the same structure without any being reality’s ultimate alphabet.

It is reasonable to consider a law good when it makes precise predictions, works in new situations, connects previously separate phenomena and allows us to identify when it can no longer be used. No criterion is sufficient alone. A very vague statement can ‘explain’ everything precisely because it excludes nothing. A relationship fitted impeccably to known data may fail at the first new observation.

The decisive question becomes: what risk does the explanation take? If every possible result can be reinterpreted as confirmation, we may have a worldview but not yet a tool for discriminating among possible worlds. A law’s power does not lie in the word’s solemnity. It also lies in the number of things it allows us to declare incompatible with it.
